h: Masques, horses and a writer ahead of her time
p: When Charles I and his queen came to Bolsover in 1634, William Cavendish pulled out all the stops. He commissioned the playwright Ben Jonson to write a masque, a sort of lavish musical show, called Love's Welcome at Bolsover, and laid on a feast that reportedly cost an eye-watering sum. It's a great example of how the castle was built as a stage for impressing powerful guests.

Cavendish himself was a fascinating character. He was a Royalist commander in the Civil War, spent years in exile on the Continent, and became one of the most famous horsemen of his age, writing a celebrated book on the art of training horses. That passion is why the Riding School exists, and why the horse displays fit so well here.

His second wife, Margaret Cavendish, deserves a mention too. She was a writer and philosopher who published poems, plays and scientific ideas at a time when women rarely did, and her book The Blazing World is often described as one of the earliest works of science fiction.
Allow around three hours to explore without rushing. The views from the walls are wonderful on a clear day, so don't forget the camera.

You're well placed for more Derbyshire history. Hardwick Hall, with its huge windows, and the ruined Hardwick Old Hall are a short drive south. Sutton Scarsdale Hall, a dramatic roofless Georgian shell, is close by too. And Creswell Crags, a limestone gorge with caves used by Ice Age people, has some of the oldest cave art found in Britain. Chesterfield's famous crooked spire is only a few miles west.
